title: Covered-Call ETFs Need an Upside Budget
meta_description: Evaluate covered-call ETFs through option mechanics, total return, distribution sources, downside risk, upside caps, taxes and portfolio fit—not yield alone.

sections.heading: The Distribution Is Payment for a Trade-Off
paragraphs: Covered-call exchange-traded funds are often marketed through a prominent distribution rate. The cash can look like bond interest or a dividend bonus added to stock ownership. It is neither automatically. The fund generally owns stocks or stock exposure and sells call options, receiving option premium while transferring some upside above a strike price for a stated period.

The opening photograph shows market charts because the product’s income is created inside an equity-and-options strategy. A call buyer pays for the right to participate above the strike under the contract terms. The seller receives premium and accepts an obligation. When the market rises sharply, the written calls can offset part of the portfolio’s gain. When the market falls, premium provides only a limited cushion.

A high distribution rate therefore does not establish high return, stable income or low risk. Cash paid to shareholders can include option income, dividends, realized gains and sometimes return of capital under tax classifications. Net asset value can fall while distributions continue. The investor must evaluate total return—price change plus distributions—not cash yield alone.

Covered-call ETFs are not inherently traps. They can implement a disciplined buy-write exposure, reduce some volatility in certain conditions and convert uncertain future upside into current premium. But usefulness depends on objective, underlying holdings, option coverage, strike selection, costs, taxes and the market regime.
The correct first question is not “How much does it pay?” It is “What economic exposure produces the payment, and which outcome am I giving up?”

Start with a household objective expressed without a product name: preserve purchasing power, fund flexible monthly spending, reduce portfolio volatility or seek long-term growth. Then ask whether selling calls advances that objective. A retiree needing dependable essential expenses may discover that a variable equity distribution is not a reserve. An accumulator may discover that a high current payout conflicts with growth. The fund should earn its place against a relevant alternative, not against zero. If the only reason is last year’s quoted yield, the analysis has not begun.

Beware language that turns a distribution target into an income promise. A manager can often maintain cash payments for a time by realizing gains, distributing option proceeds or returning capital, but the portfolio’s value and future earning base may change. Ask what must happen for both the payout and net asset value to remain healthy. If the answer requires favorable markets, elevated volatility or repeated gains, describe the payment as market-dependent. The same discipline applies when the quoted distribution exceeds the underlying portfolio’s ordinary dividend yield by a wide margin: identify the option obligation and capital source that bridge the difference.

sections.heading: Separate the ETF Wrapper From the Option Strategy
paragraphs: An ETF pools investor money and issues shares trading on an exchange. Its portfolio, adviser, fees, creation-and-redemption process and market price are part of the wrapper. A covered-call mandate is the strategy used within that wrapper. Two funds bearing the same label can own different stocks, write options on different underlyings and pursue different distribution policies.

The [[S1|SEC’s ETF overview]] explains that each ETF share represents an interest in a portfolio and its income, while ETFs carry market, trading and strategy risks. Shares can trade above or below net asset value, and distributions can change. Registration does not mean an agency approves the strategy or protects its market value.

Read whether the fund owns individual securities and writes calls on them, owns a portfolio while writing index calls, holds another ETF, or obtains exposure through derivatives. Index options may settle in cash; equity options can involve delivery. The prospectus describes the actual mechanism, collateral and counterparties.

Check how much of the portfolio is overwritten. A fund writing calls against one hundred percent of notional exposure behaves differently from one covering a quarter or half. Partial coverage retains more uncapped participation but generally collects less premium. Coverage can also vary with market conditions.
Do not infer the strategy from the ticker or trailing payout. Map underlying exposure, call coverage, option reference, tenor and strike rule before comparing funds.

Also distinguish net asset value from exchange price. Authorized participants and arbitrage often keep them close, but spreads and premiums or discounts can widen during stress or in less liquid funds. Use a limit order when appropriate and inspect average spread, market depth and trading time. The liquidity of an ETF share is related to, but not identical with, screen volume because underlying holdings and option markets also affect execution. A strategy with liquid large-cap stocks can still incur implementation costs when rolling many contracts under volatile conditions.

sections.heading: Draw the One-Period Payoff Before Reading the Yield
paragraphs: A simplified covered call owns an asset at $100 and sells a call with a $105 strike for a $3 premium. At expiration, ignoring fees, dividends and tax, the premium shifts the break-even down to $97. If the asset finishes at $80, the combined position loses $17. The strategy cushioned the loss by $3; it did not eliminate the $20 decline.

If the asset ends at $100, the underlying has no change and the premium produces a $3 gain. At $105, the underlying gains $5 and premium adds $3. Above $105, the call’s obligation offsets additional underlying gains, leaving the simplified result capped near $8. Path, settlement and fund implementation can change real results, but the exchange is visible.

FINRA [[S2|defines a covered call]] as selling a call while owning the underlying stock. The seller’s maximum option profit is the premium, while assignment can require selling the shares. A fund structure can use index options and portfolio-level mechanics, yet the same economic principle remains: premium is received in return for limiting an outcome.

The term covered refers to the call obligation being supported by underlying exposure. It does not mean the shareholder is covered against market loss. If the portfolio drops fifty percent, a few percent of premium cannot make the position safe.

Recreate a payoff at several underlying prices using the fund’s approximate strike and premium. If the investor dislikes the capped-upside region or cannot tolerate the downside region, the distribution rate cannot repair the mismatch.

Real funds repeat the trade, so one-period diagrams are necessary but incomplete. After a decline, the next call may be written at a lower market level; a rebound above that new strike can be capped before the portfolio recovers its former value. Managers may close calls early, roll to another strike or vary coverage, changing realized results. Record whether the methodology holds to expiration or acts before it. The repeated path determines shareholder experience, while a static payoff diagram only explains the current contract.

sections.heading: A Distribution Is Not the Same as Earned Yield
paragraphs: Fund cash distributions can come from several sources. Stock dividends are paid by portfolio companies. Option premiums are transaction proceeds whose economic result depends on later settlement or closing. Realized gains can arise from securities or options. Return of capital may represent tax classification of a payment that is not currently treated as income; it is not automatically benign or harmful.

Distribution yield is commonly annualized from a recent payment or measured over twelve months and divided by market price or net asset value. A monthly payment boosted by unusual volatility can produce an eye-catching annualized figure that does not persist. Confirm the issuer’s definition and whether the displayed rate is historical, indicated or targeted.

A fund can pay $10 while its net asset value declines $12, leaving a negative total return before tax. Conversely, a lower distribution can accompany stronger wealth growth. Reinvested-distribution charts are more useful than payout alone, but they still depend on period and benchmark.

Section 19(a) notices can provide estimates of distribution sources for certain funds, while final tax reporting can differ. Read annual reports and Form 1099 information rather than assuming every monthly dollar has the same tax character.

Build a cash-source table for the fund and a personal spending rule. If distributions are needed for expenses, decide what happens when they fall; do not design fixed obligations around a discretionary fund payout.

Watch the ex-distribution date. A fund’s net asset value generally falls by roughly the amount distributed, all else equal, because cash leaves the portfolio. Receiving one dollar and seeing the fund value adjust down by one dollar does not create one dollar of wealth. Economic value comes from portfolio results before and after that transfer. This is why automatically reinvested total-return data and account statements are essential. A payment can meet a spending need while still consuming part of capital; name that choice honestly.

sections.heading: Measure the Upside Budget You Are Selling
paragraphs: Every call-writing program spends an upside budget. At-the-money calls usually collect more premium but begin capping gains sooner. Out-of-the-money calls collect less and preserve a band of appreciation before the cap. Shorter expirations reset more often; longer contracts lock terms for more time. Volatility and interest rates affect premium.

The strike may be selected by percentage moneyness, option delta, income target or manager judgment. A thirty-delta call is not “thirty percent upside.” Delta is an option sensitivity measure that changes as price, time and volatility change. Read the methodology rather than translating a technical input into a guaranteed probability.

The [[S3|Cboe BXM factsheet]] describes a hypothetical portfolio long the S&P 500 Index and selling successive one-month at-the-money calls. Its payoff illustration states the core exchange: option premium in return for an upside cap. The index is a benchmark, not an investable fund and not proof that every implementation will match.

Estimate how much equity exposure is overwritten and the distance to the strike. A full overwrite near the money can lag sharply during persistent rallies. A partial, out-of-the-money program may keep more upside but provide less distributable premium.
Call premium should be compared with foregone gains over full cycles, not celebrated in isolation during quiet months.

Create a rally test using the actual methodology. Estimate results if the underlying rises five, ten or twenty percent before the next roll, then repeat when only part of the portfolio is covered. Include premium but avoid assuming every contract earns its quoted amount after closing and transaction costs. The test reveals whether the strategy’s expected lag is tolerable. Investors often accept a cap abstractly but regret it when a familiar benchmark surges; a written upside budget makes the opportunity cost visible before that emotional moment.

sections.heading: Downside Risk Still Belongs to the Shareholder
paragraphs: The midpoint photograph shows charts under a magnifying glass because due diligence must inspect the loss side. Covered calls generally leave substantial equity downside. Premium lowers the break-even for one period, but the cushion resets and can be small relative to a crash. The fund can decline while calls expire profitably.

Underlying concentration matters. A fund holding a narrow technology, single-stock or high-volatility portfolio may advertise rich premiums precisely because expected movement and risk are high. Option markets do not normally provide large recurring premium without pricing uncertainty.

Some products add leverage, synthetic exposures or complex counterparties. The SEC [[S4|warns]] that ETFs using options and other derivatives inherit the risks of those instruments. Although an ETF shareholder’s direct loss is generally limited to the investment absent margin, the fund can still experience severe net-asset-value declines.

Check the maximum drawdown, recovery period and behavior during rapid rebounds. A call strategy can cushion part of the fall, then surrender upside during recovery because new calls were written after prices dropped. Sequence matters to an investor withdrawing distributions.
Use the fund as equity risk unless evidence supports a more precise category. Do not substitute it one-for-one for insured cash or high-quality short-duration reserves.

Examine how distributions interact with drawdown. Withdrawing cash during a decline leaves fewer assets positioned for recovery, and a fixed percentage of original capital becomes a growing percentage of the remaining balance. Reinvestment can preserve shares but defeats the immediate-income purpose. Model both paths: distributions spent and distributions reinvested. For a retiree, include sequence risk; for an accumulator, include taxes and reinvestment. A fund that recovered on a total-return chart may not restore an account from which every payment was withdrawn.

Review tail risks outside the payoff diagram. Trading may be disrupted, an option market can become less liquid, tax rules can change and a fund may close or alter its mandate. Index-option settlement can behave differently from delivery of individual shares. Counterparty exposure matters for over-the-counter contracts, while collateral and cash drag can affect return. None of these details means the product should be rejected automatically; they mean “covered” is not a complete risk description. The investor needs the prospectus risk section and current holdings before relying on historical smoothness.

sections.heading: Volatility Can Raise Premium and Complicate the Result
paragraphs: Option premium tends to rise when implied volatility is higher, all else equal. That can support a larger distribution, but volatility also signals a wider range of expected outcomes. Rich premium is compensation for accepting an obligation in an uncertain market, not free income created by an ETF manager.

The strategy often looks relatively attractive when markets move sideways, rise gradually below strikes or decline modestly. It can lag in strong rallies because calls cap gains. It can lose substantially in deep selloffs because premium is limited. A whipsaw can be difficult when calls are reset after declines and the market rebounds quickly.

Compare results across bull markets, selloffs, rebounds and quiet periods. One favorable year can coincide with exactly the regime suited to option selling. A trailing yield measured during high implied volatility may fall when conditions normalize.

Index backtests require caution. Methodology may use theoretical prices, assume disciplined rolls and omit fund expenses, taxes or trading frictions. A live fund can differ through execution, cash holdings, sampling and distribution policy.
Do not forecast next year’s payout by multiplying this month’s distribution by twelve without understanding the volatility and realized-option environment that produced it.

Separate implied volatility from realized volatility. Option prices reflect the market’s forward-looking expectations and supply-demand conditions; the movement that eventually occurs can be smaller or larger. Selling options is not a mechanical harvest of a permanent volatility premium without risk. The fund repeatedly accepts outcomes across changing prices. Review whether management targets a constant coverage, a constant distribution or a risk measure, because each objective can force different trades when volatility jumps. No single premium level describes the whole cycle.

sections.heading: Benchmark Total Return, Volatility and Drawdown Together
paragraphs: Choose a benchmark that matches the underlying opportunity set. A large-cap covered-call fund might be compared with its equity index, a buy-write strategy index and a blended portfolio reflecting the investor’s alternative. Comparing only to a bond yield or savings rate hides the fund’s equity risk and foregone appreciation.

Use total return with distributions reinvested for accumulation decisions. For spending decisions, also model cash withdrawn and ending net asset value. A stable-looking income stream can accompany shrinking capital, changing how much future income the same distribution rate can support.

The Cboe factsheet reports long-history statistics for its hypothetical BXM index, including annualized return, volatility and maximum drawdown. Those figures describe one at-the-money index methodology and include backtested history before launch where stated. They are context, not a projection for a specific ETF.

Risk-adjusted ratios can help but should not erase path. Examine calendar returns, capture in rising and falling markets, worst rolling periods and recovery time. Confirm that the benchmark begins on the same date and uses the same reinvestment convention.
A strategy can lower measured volatility and still be unsuitable if the investor needs strong upside to fund a distant goal. Risk is failure of the plan, not one statistic.

Use share-class and inception-aware data. A fund launched after a difficult period cannot be credited with surviving it through a hypothetical index alone. Conversely, a young live record does not establish failure. Separate benchmark history, backtest history and fund history in every table. Deduct the fund’s expenses and account for implementation differences when setting expectations. If an issuer compares its fund with a price-only index while distributions are included for the fund, rebuild the comparison using total return for both sides.

Build a compact scorecard with no more than a dozen fields: starting and ending net asset value, distributions, total return, benchmark total return, annualized volatility, maximum drawdown, upside capture, downside capture, expense ratio, average spread and tax character. Use identical dates and note whether figures are market-price or net-asset-value based. Update it annually rather than selecting whichever period flatters the holding. When a covered-call fund trails in a rally, the scorecard should show whether the lag approximates the accepted cap. When it falls, it should show whether premium delivered the expected cushion. Unexplained behavior requires disclosure review before any conclusion about manager skill. Preserve each scorecard so changing market regimes can be compared without relying on memory, advertising or the latest unusually large monthly payment over several complete market cycles.

sections.heading: Fund Design Creates Different Covered-Call Experiences
paragraphs: Review the underlying portfolio first. Broad-market, dividend-stock, technology, small-company and single-stock exposures have different concentration, dividend and volatility profiles before any option is written. The option overlay modifies that base; it does not replace it.

Then inspect the option reference. Writing index calls against a non-identical stock portfolio introduces basis risk: the option and holdings may not move together. Writing calls on individual holdings can create assignment and turnover differences. Synthetic approaches can add counterparty and collateral considerations.

Check tenor, strike, coverage, roll schedule and discretion. Daily, weekly and monthly programs react differently to market paths. Rules-based funds can be transparent but mechanically sell during unfavorable conditions; active managers may adapt but add discretion and evaluation difficulty.

Distribution targets can influence behavior. A fund attempting a fixed monthly percentage may distribute more than current net economic income, while another lets payouts fluctuate. Read whether the policy is managed, variable or tied to option proceeds.
Finally compare expense ratio, trading spreads, assets, volume, premium-discount history and closure policy. Strategy complexity does not excuse high unexplained cost.

Read the schedule of investments rather than relying only on strategy prose. It can reveal whether calls are exchange traded or over the counter, which index or securities underlie them, their notional amount, current value and expiration. Financial statements show realized and unrealized derivative results over a reporting period, though they remain backward-looking. Material borrowing, collateral arrangements or affiliated funds deserve attention. If the disclosure cannot be translated into a simple exposure map, pause before assigning the product a major portfolio role.

sections.heading: Taxes Can Change the Spendable Income
paragraphs: Tax character depends on the fund’s structure, holdings, option types, transactions and the investor’s account. Payments labeled distributions during the year can receive different final classifications. Option gains may be treated differently from qualified dividends, and return of capital can reduce cost basis until later disposition. General labels are not personal tax advice.

Index options may receive different federal treatment from equity options under applicable rules. Funds can use tax-management techniques, but marketing phrases such as tax efficient require verification in reports and personal circumstances.

Compare after-tax total return, not headline cash. A strategy producing frequent short-term gains in a taxable account may leave less spendable wealth than a lower-distribution alternative. A retirement account changes current taxation but has contribution, withdrawal and required-distribution rules.

Review the prospectus tax section, annual report, distribution notices and final Form 1099. If a payment includes return of capital, track adjusted basis even when the broker reports it. State taxes can differ.

A qualified tax professional should evaluate large allocations, loss harvesting, retirement withdrawals or unfamiliar option classifications. Do not choose a complex fund solely to pursue a tax label.

Return of capital deserves a two-part review. First ask the tax question: does the classification defer recognition by reducing basis? Then ask the economic question: did the portfolio earn enough total return to replace the cash paid? A tax-deferred classification does not prove destructive capital return, and a payment labeled income does not prove sustainable wealth. Keep these questions separate. Tax lots, holding period and state rules can change the investor’s after-tax result even when two people own the same fund.

sections.heading: Decide Whether Current Cash Is Worth Less Future Upside
paragraphs: Covered-call funds may fit an investor who deliberately values current cash and accepts capped participation on a defined slice of equity exposure. They may be less suitable for an early accumulator whose plan relies on decades of equity growth, or for anyone treating the payout as guaranteed principal-safe income.

Write an upside budget: what fraction of equity gains can the plan surrender during strong markets without threatening the goal? Then set an allocation limit consistent with that budget. Avoid replacing the entire equity portfolio merely because one fund’s recent distribution is high.

Match cash need to cash source. Essential near-term spending should have reserves not dependent on equity markets. Distributions from an option-income fund can supplement a flexible spending category, but cuts or net-asset-value loss need a contingency.

Consider simpler alternatives: selling shares from a diversified portfolio under a withdrawal policy, combining stocks and high-quality bonds, or using a smaller covered-call sleeve. Cash generated by selling shares is not inherently worse than cash labeled income; total return, tax and risk determine the result.
Document why the allocation exists, which benchmark tests it and what condition triggers reduction or removal.

Size the allocation through a failure test. Assume the distribution falls thirty percent, net asset value declines twenty-five percent and the broad equity benchmark rebounds faster. Can essential spending, rebalancing and long-term goals continue without selling at an unwanted time? If not, reduce dependence or strengthen reserves. Also test the opposite regime: a multi-year rally in which the covered-call sleeve lags. Opportunity cost is not an emergency, but it can cause strategy abandonment unless the original reason remains strong.

Compare the fund with a self-funded withdrawal plan using the same starting assets. In one path, the investor receives the fund distribution; in another, a diversified portfolio periodically sells a small number of shares. Both can reduce units or capital available for future growth, and both face market sequence. The relevant differences are allocation, taxes, costs, discipline and the option overlay—not whether the cash arrived with an income label. This comparison often reveals that the real decision is how much equity upside to retain and how spending will adjust during weak markets.

sections.heading: Run a Prospectus-to-Portfolio Review
paragraphs: The final photograph shows financial documents being reviewed because the decision belongs in the prospectus, reports and portfolio plan—not in a yield leaderboard. Start with objective and principal strategy. Record holdings, option reference, coverage, strike method, tenor, roll schedule, distribution policy, fee and principal risks.

Inspect the latest holdings and option positions when available. Compare stated method with actual exposure: notional coverage, cash level, expiration and moneyness. Review several distribution notices and annual tax classifications, recognizing estimates can change.

Calculate total return and ending net asset value over matched periods. Compare with the underlying benchmark and a relevant buy-write index. Examine rally capture, downside capture, drawdown and rebound. Explain any large difference before investing.

Set a review calendar rather than reacting to each payment. Quarterly, verify strategy drift, coverage and distribution sources. Annually, reassess portfolio role, taxes, costs and whether forgone upside remains acceptable.

A covered-call ETF becomes understandable when the investor can state the full bargain: which assets are owned, which calls are sold, how much upside is transferred, what downside remains, where cash comes from and how success will be measured.

Write the conclusion in plain language before purchase: “I am allocating this percentage of the portfolio to own this exposure, sell calls on approximately this amount, seek flexible cash, and accept these capped gains and equity losses.” Add the expected holding period and exit rule. After purchase, reconcile brokerage distributions with issuer notices and final tax forms. If the fund changes its index, overwrite policy, fee or distribution method, treat that as a new decision—not a cosmetic update to an old holding.

Finish with an operational check. Identify who monitors notices, where tax records are stored, how distributions are directed and whether automatic reinvestment matches the intended use. Confirm limit-order practice and avoid placing a large trade when spreads are unusually wide. Record the first review after at least one option roll and one distribution, but do not infer a cycle from a single month. Over time, compare actual premium, payout, net asset value and benchmark results with the written thesis. A repeated unexplained gap is a reason to investigate, not to increase the allocation for a higher yield.

summary: A covered-call ETF generally owns stocks or stock exposure and sells calls, collecting premium while giving up some gains above a strike for a stated period. Define the household objective before evaluating any distribution rate or ticker. Test the full trade-off.

The distribution is payment from an investment process, not free income added to ordinary equity return. ETF market price, net asset value and underlying liquidity are related but not identical. Test the full trade-off.

Separate the ETF wrapper from the strategy. Funds can differ in holdings, option reference, coverage, strike, tenor, roll schedule and distribution policy. Repeated rolls create path dependence that a single expiration diagram cannot display. Test the full trade-off.

Draw a one-period payoff. Premium creates a limited cushion, but the underlying portfolio can still suffer substantial loss. Cash leaving on an ex-distribution date is a transfer, not instant new wealth. Test the full trade-off.

The word covered means underlying exposure supports the call obligation; it does not mean the shareholder is protected against a market decline. Stress-test strong rallies so the opportunity cost is understood before it arrives. Test the full trade-off.

Inspect distribution sources. Cash can reflect dividends, option activity, realized gains and tax-classified return of capital. Model distributions both spent and reinvested during a prolonged portfolio drawdown. Test the full trade-off.

Distribution yield is not total return. Add price change and distributions, then compare matched periods and reinvestment conventions. Option premium reflects implied uncertainty; the eventual realized movement can differ. Test the full trade-off.

Every program sells an upside budget. At-the-money and higher-coverage calls usually cap more appreciation than partial or farther out-of-the-money programs. Keep live fund results, benchmark history and hypothetical backtests clearly separated. Test the full trade-off.

Rich option premium often accompanies higher expected movement. It is compensation for an obligation in an uncertain market. Verify current contracts and notional exposure in holdings and financial statements. Test the full trade-off.

Covered-call approaches can perform relatively well in sideways or modest markets and lag during strong rallies. They can still lose heavily in selloffs. Separate the tax classification of a payment from its economic sustainability. Test the full trade-off.

Compare with the underlying equity benchmark, a relevant buy-write index and the investor’s actual alternative. Test payout cuts, equity declines and prolonged benchmark outperformance before sizing. Test the full trade-off.

Review total return, volatility, maximum drawdown, recovery time, upside capture and downside capture together. Write the allocation purpose, accepted trade-offs, review date and exit trigger. Test the full trade-off.

Look through the label to underlying concentration, basis risk, counterparty exposure, collateral and any leverage or synthetic construction. Never treat an option-income fund as a substitute for insured emergency cash. Test the full trade-off.

Compare expense ratio, spreads, premium-discount history, assets, trading volume and implementation differences. Do not compare distribution percentages without matching dates and calculation methods. Test the full trade-off.

Tax character depends on structure and transactions. Estimated distribution classifications can differ from final reporting. Read the issuer definition of every displayed yield before annualizing it yourself. Test the full trade-off.

Essential spending needs reserves that do not depend on equity distributions. Build a contingency for payout cuts and capital decline. Check whether quoted performance deducts fees and assumes distributions are reinvested. Test the full trade-off.

Consider whether selling shares from a diversified total-return portfolio or using a stock-bond mix better meets the same cash need. Use official disclosure and final tax documents instead of relying on marketing labels. Test the full trade-off.

Use a written upside budget, allocation limit, benchmark and review trigger rather than selecting from a yield leaderboard. A suitable allocation is one whose upside cap and downside remain acceptable together. Test the full trade-off.

faq.question: Are covered-call ETF distributions guaranteed?
faq.answer: No. Option premiums, dividends, realized results and distribution policies change, and the fund can reduce its payment.

faq.question: Does a covered call protect against a market crash?
faq.answer: Only modestly through premium received. Substantial underlying losses generally remain.

faq.question: Why can a covered-call ETF lag in a bull market?
faq.answer: Written calls can offset gains above their strikes, especially when coverage is high and strikes are near the market.

faq.question: Is return of capital always bad?
faq.answer: No. It is a tax classification that requires context. It may reduce basis and can coexist with different economic outcomes.

faq.question: Should I compare the payout with a bond yield?
faq.answer: Not by itself. Covered-call funds usually retain equity risk. Compare total return, drawdown and the full portfolio role.

faq.question: Are all covered-call ETFs similar?
faq.answer: No. Holdings, option reference, coverage, tenor, strikes, management and payout policies can produce materially different behavior.

faq.question: Where should I verify the strategy?
faq.answer: Use the prospectus, statement of additional information, reports, holdings, option positions, distribution notices and tax forms.

glossary.definition: Contract giving its buyer the right to buy an underlying asset under specified terms while obligating the seller if exercised.
Call sold while the seller holds supporting underlying exposure.
Price at which the option holder can transact under the contract.
Amount paid by the buyer and received by the seller for the option.
Relationship between an option strike and underlying market level.
Share of portfolio exposure against which calls are written.
Per-share value of fund assets minus liabilities.
Price or net-asset-value change plus distributions over a period.
Distribution amount classified for tax purposes as returning investor basis rather than current income or gain.
Benchmark modeling ownership of an underlying portfolio and systematic sale of calls.
